svg.aria-label: Diagram: the Azure landing zone, showing its two components of platform landing zone and application landing zones, the baseline management group hierarchy from intermediate root through Platform with Security Management Connectivity and Identity, and Landing zones with Corp Online and Local, plus Sandboxes and Decommissioned, the depth guidance of six levels allowed against three or four recommended, and five things the guidance explicitly tells you not to do
svg.title: The Azure landing zone is the reference answer to the whole of Phase 1, and its most useful content is the list of things it tells you not to build
svg.text: Two components, one hierarchy, and a list of things not to do.
The platform team owns the foundation. Workload teams own their own landing zones. The boundary between them is the whole design.
Platform landing zone
The centralized foundation: governance, security and
shared resources for every workload.
A management group hierarchy, centralized resources,
and a way to hand landing zones to workload teams.
One per Entra tenant for most organizations.
Application landing zones
Where workload teams deploy, inside the guardrails the
platform sets.
One per workload, containing every environment that
workload needs — each environment one or more
subscriptions.
The baseline hierarchy, and what each group is for
Intermediate root
Directly under tenant root, with your own prefix, so the
tenant root group itself is never used.
Platform
Security · Management · Connectivity · Identity
one subscription each
Landing zones
Corp — needs corporate or hybrid connectivity via the hub
Online — direct internet, or no virtual network at all
Sandboxes
Local — Azure Local clusters, with different policy needs
Sandboxes — isolated, deliberately less restrictive
Decommissioned
Cancelled landing zones move here, and Azure deletes them after 30-60 days
A management group tree supports six levels of depth, and the recommendation is three to four — two levels of headroom you are asked
not to spend. Every new subscription lands under tenant root by default, which is why a default group is configured to catch them.
The five things the guidance tells you not to do — each one an instinct
Do not mirror the org chart
management groups are for policy assignment, not billing or reporting lines
Do not give app teams RBAC at MG scope
over-permissioning, plus the added risk from inheritance — grant at the subscription
or resource group they actually need
Do not make dev, test and prod groups
separate them into subscriptions inside the same management group instead
Do not model regions
unless data residency or sovereignty requires it — then, and only then, by location
Do not load the root group with policy
limit assignments there, or you debug inherited policy in every group below
And one default worth changing on day one: by default any principal in the tenant can create management groups under the root. Enabling
RBAC authorization in the hierarchy settings overrides that. Platform teams that do need management group scope should hold it through
Privileged Identity Management, so the access exists only while it is being used.
Sources: What is an Azure landing zone, and the management groups design area of the Cloud Adoption Framework, on Microsoft Learn.
